substitution.claim: USGS: niobium and tungsten can replace it in carbides; aluminium, ceramics and niobium in capacitors; several metals in corrosion-resistant and high-temperature uses - but with performance loss or higher cost.

EU SCRREEN2: in superalloys, swapping tantalum out would dramatically change the alloy, and a certified jet-engine alloy takes many years to requalify; tantalum is a small cost share, so substitution is unlikely.

EU SCRREEN2: most capacitors already avoid tantalum on cost; it remains the only reliable option where long-term reliability, small size or safety matters (e.g. ABS brakes, airbag triggers, satellites). Niobium, ceramic and aluminium alternatives are larger or less tolerant of heat.
RFC Ambrian: tungsten, molybdenum or titanium could in principle replace it as the copper barrier in chips, but tantalum is still preferred for its stability with copper and adhesion to silicon.
USGS: aluminium, glass, paper, plastic or tin-free steel replace tin in cans; epoxy resins can replace solder in some uses.
USGS: gold-clad base metals economise on gold in electronics and jewellery; palladium, platinum and silver can substitute generally.
US: tantalum is on the final 2025 US List of Critical Minerals (60 minerals); so is tin; gold is not.
EU: tantalum is on the 2023 EU critical raw materials list (34) but not on the strategic list; tin and gold are on neither.

Recycling cannot fill the gap quickly: end-of-life tantalum recycling is under 1% because capacitors are tiny and tantalum ends up in copper-smelter slag; recycled supply (mostly manufacturing scrap) is 25-30%.
Tantalum's useful properties: very high melting point (3,020 C, fourth highest), high density, strong corrosion resistance, and a stable oxide film that acts as the capacitor dielectric.
Oeko-Institut (2012): tantalum in German notebooks was effectively not recovered at all (100% lost at collection or treatment), because precious-metal refining cannot recover it.

caveats: Production figures are USGS estimates in metal content. Rwanda's tantalum 'production' is derived from its exports with an assumed 26% Ta2O5 grade, so it includes DRC ore smuggled into Rwanda (UN GoE). DRC + Rwanda together is the more honest unit for the Kivu supply.

About half of DRC's 2024 tantalum (est. 630 t of 1,270 t) is modelled as tantalum contained in cassiterite, not coltan; and 47% of DRC's declared coltan comes from Haut-Katanga, not the conflict-affected east.

The ~15% Rubaya share is repeated by Global Witness, IPIS and Reuters without a stated method; the UN Group of Experts gives volumes (120 t/month) but no share. Our volume-based cross-check gives roughly 9-19% (about 12% at Rwanda's assumed 26% Ta2O5 grade).

Tantalum end-use shares are an analyst estimate (RFC Ambrian, 2025, citing T.I.C. and USGS). T.I.C.'s own statistics are member-only; the last public T.I.C.-based split (2020) gives capacitors ~36%, electronics ~50%, metallurgy ~25%. Shares vary by source by several points.
ITA tin-use split slide is undated; assumed to be 2024 data (presented May 2025).
WGC gold shares are of 'gold demand' excluding OTC (4,999.4 t in 2025). Investment and central-bank buying (61%) dominate; technology is only ~6.5%.

Per-product content is thin: no verified current figure for tantalum or tin per smartphone or laptop, or tantalum per car. The Bookhagen et al. (2020) smartphone gold figure (16.8 mg) is unverified (paywalled). The USGS 34 mg gold figure is for a 2005 phone.
Trade data are customs records, not proof of mine origin (PROJECT_RULES 10). Argus 2025 China-Rwanda figure (2,865 t) and Global Witness 2024 figure (2,286 t) are gross ore weights.

No credible public source found for share of world tantalum capacitors made in each country, or for China's share of world tantalum processing capacity; RFC Ambrian's 'China ~30% of consumption' is the closest proxy.
